summary: Akram Baharlouei, a machine learning engineer at Altos Labs, discusses the engineering challenges of building foundation models for single-cell biology from a non-biologist's perspective. He begins with the Yamanaka factor example: in 2006, Shinya Yamanaka discovered four transcription factors capable of reprogramming old skin cells back to embryonic stem cell-like states, work that earned a Nobel Prize in 2012. This enables partial programming—changing a cell's age without changing its type—with the first reprogramming medicine (OSK) reportedly entering human testing around 2026. The broader vision is modeling from single cells to tissues to organs to entire humans, supported by initiatives like the Human Cell Atlas, with concepts like virtual cells, virtual tissues, and digital twins. Drug development faces declining productivity despite technology advances, with pipelines taking up to 10 years, costing billions, and acceptance rates around 5%. Baharlouei then covers measurement modalities: genome (DNA sequencing, same across cells), RNA-seq/transcriptomics (gene expression profiles of ~20,000 genes), proteomics (important but hard to measure, low throughput), and morphology (cell shape via imaging). RNA-seq dominates foundation model training due to scalability, with datasets ranging from tens of millions to potentially 1 billion cells. However, single-cell data is inherently noisy and heterogeneous—identical cells measured twice yield different readings due to both biological (burst-like cell cycle changes, snapshot measurement from a continuous process) and technical (different labs, machines) reasons. Baharlouei reviews transformer-based models like SCGPT and Informer that treat cells as sentences and genes as tokens, using BERT-style masking to predict gene counts. These models compress data into latent vectors, losing information, and comprehensive benchmarking (two NeurIPS papers) shows they are expensive to train yet often underperform, sometimes beaten by simple linear models. He also mentions CPADR, an autoencoder-based model that maps to the mean rather than understanding the distribution, evaluated with MMD scores. Flow matching-based models like PrimeFlow, which predict data distributions starting from Gaussian noise rather than compressing into latent vectors, appear to perform better than autoregressive approaches. In his conclusions, Baharlouei emphasizes three key takeaways: single-cell biology is important for cellular rejuvenation, digital humans, and drug development; RNA-seq is the most available modality at scale but data quality must improve to better reflect real organisms rather than just scaling data as-is; and flow matching models currently perform best for single-cell data by matching distributions. To scale models that generalize to unseen data, both massive data scaling and improved data quality are essential. He references three papers: SCGPT, perturbation benchmarking from NeurIPS, and PrimeFlow.

sections.title: Introduction and Yamanaka Factors
sections.summary: Baharlouei introduces himself as an ML engineer at Altos Labs, a biotech startup focused on cellular rejuvenation. He presents the Yamanaka factor example: four transcription factors discovered in 2006 that can reprogram old skin cells to embryonic stem cell-like states, earning a Nobel Prize in 2012. This enables partial programming—changing cell age without changing type—with the first reprogramming medicine (OSK) reportedly entering human testing around 2026.

sections.title: Modeling Vision and Drug Development Challenges
sections.summary: The vision is to model from single cells to tissues to organs to entire humans, supported by initiatives like the Human Cell Atlas. Concepts include virtual cell, virtual tissue, virtual human, and digital twins. Drug development faces declining productivity despite technology advances, with pipelines taking up to 10 years, costing billions, and ~5% acceptance rates. Innovation is needed across the entire pipeline, not just research and development.

sections.title: Measuring Single Cells: Modalities
sections.summary: Different modalities measure different aspects of single cells: genome (DNA sequencing, same across cells), RNA-seq/transcriptomics (gene expression profiles of ~20,000 genes), proteomics (important but hard to measure, low throughput), and morphology (cell shape via imaging, useful for spatial context). RNA-seq dominates foundation model training due to scalability, with datasets from tens of millions to 1 billion cells.

sections.title: Challenges with Single-Cell Data
sections.summary: Single-cell data is inherently noisy and heterogeneous. Identical cells measured twice give different readings due to biological reasons (burst-like cell cycle changes, snapshots from continuous processes) and technical reasons (different labs, machines). The data is high-dimensional and multi-state. Quantum computing may eventually be a natural fit, but current AI is the focus.

sections.title: Transformer-Based Foundation Models
sections.summary: Models like SCGPT and Informer treat cells as sentences and genes as tokens, using BERT-style masking to predict gene counts. They compress data into latent vectors for downstream tasks like cell type prediction and perturbation response modeling, but lose information in compression. Two NeurIPS benchmarking papers show these models are expensive to train yet often underperform, sometimes beaten by simple linear models, and do not match performance seen in language or imaging domains.

sections.title: Flow Matching-Based Models
sections.summary: Flow matching-based models like PrimeFlow predict data distributions starting from Gaussian noise rather than compressing into latent vectors. Early results show PrimeFlow better matching ground truth distributions compared to autoregressive models, suggesting flow matching may be a more promising approach for single-cell foundation models.

sections.title: Conclusions and Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Baharlouei concludes with three takeaways: single-cell biology is important for cellular rejuvenation, digital humans, and drug development; RNA-seq is the most scalable modality but data quality must improve to reflect real organisms rather than just scaling data as-is; and flow matching models currently perform best for single-cell data by matching distributions. He notes that CPADR, an autoencoder-based model, maps to the mean rather than understanding distributions, evaluated with MMD scores. To scale models that generalize to unseen data, both massive data scaling and improved measurement quality are essential. He references three papers: SCGPT, perturbation benchmarking from NeurIPS, and PrimeFlow.
